_comment_1: ATOMIC GRANULARITY ONLY. One row per requirement, not per chapter. A 14-day project should produce on the order of 100 rows. If your row count is implausibly low for project age, the loop will self-terminate before the product is good. This is the Flatline failure mode.
_comment_2: Allowed status values: not_started | partial | done. Every row should carry implementationRefs and testRefs once status >= partial. followupRefs link to F-NNN entries in FOLLOWUPS.html.

rows.requirement: V1 presents VibePinball as one polished 3D web-native table named Silverball Social.
Ball, flipper, table, ramp, lane, nudge, tilt, drain, and multiball behavior are authored as a physical simulation.
The table visual theme reads as a classic arcade cabinet with league-night Silverball Social flavor.
The default camera keeps the playfield readable in a fixed tilted 3D cabinet view.
A normal game targets a 3-5 minute three-ball session with fast restart and clear final score.
V1 success criteria are visible in the GDD and can be checked before release.
The playfield includes sloped boundaries, side walls, apron, drain, main flippers, inlanes, outlanes, shooter lane, and trough.
The lower playfield includes flippers, slingshots, inlanes, outlanes, rollover sensors, and central drain.
The upper playfield includes bumper nest, rollover lanes, skill-shot lane, and a return path.
The table includes at least one aimable ramp and one aimable orbit path.
A visible target bank advances lock progress and exposes hit, lit, and completed states.
A readable lock device captures or represents locked balls for multiball qualification.
The rendered scene includes cabinet, rails, plunger housing, speaker or DMD area, and arcade hall context.
The game runs a fixed-step Rapier 3D world with stable table-slope gravity.
The pinball is a dynamic spherical rigid body with tuned restitution, friction, spin, and velocity caps.
Flippers transfer physical force through bodies or joints and support held, released, and rapid-tap states.
Walls, posts, rubbers, lanes, rollovers, drain, targets, saucers, ramps, and bumpers use explicit colliders or sensors.
Bumpers and slingshots apply readable impulses and emit scoring, audio, lamp, and device events.
The plunger maps analog charge to launch impulse across a useful skill-shot range.
Nudging applies table-relative impulse and repeated excessive nudges trigger tilt warnings and tilt.
Drain and trough logic detects ball loss, counts bonus, serves next ball, and ends completed games.
Multiball uses multiple real active ball bodies with independent scoring and drain accounting.
Gameplay input is normalized into action state independent of keyboard, touch, or gamepad source.
Keyboard defaults cover flippers, plunger, nudges, start, pause, restart, confirm, and back.
Touch controls provide large flipper regions, analog plunger control, and explicit nudge controls.
Gamepad controls map flippers, plunger, nudges, pause, restart, confirm, and back.
Flipper and plunger input are responsive on the next simulation tick and do not drop quick taps during frame drops.
Active play controls prevent unsafe browser scrolling or focus loss while menus remain accessible.
The start and pause states show concise device-aware control reminders.
The game runs a three-ball session with bonus after each drain and final score after ball three.
Base scoring assigns explicit values to bumpers, slings, lanes, rollovers, targets, ramps, orbits, locks, jackpots, bonus, and multiball.
Analog launch can award a skill shot through a lit lane and then resets to normal play.
Completing the target bank advances visible lock qualification state.
A qualified lock shot captures or records locked balls and serves replacement balls when needed.
Multiball launches multiple active balls, lights jackpots, and ends when one active ball remains.
Multiball jackpots and super jackpot state are short, visible, and achievable in normal play.
Bonus count awards lane, target, bumper, and mode progress after non-tilted drains.
Tilt disables flippers and scoring for the current ball, cancels bonus, and clears on the next ball.
Default rules tuning is fair but demanding and rewards accurate shots, catches, plunger skill, and nudge discipline.
The default camera is fixed and shows the full playfield without chasing the ball.
Responsive framing keeps the ball and flippers readable on desktop, tablet, and phone viewports.
Three.js renders cabinet, playfield, ball, devices, lamps, DMD or HUD, and arcade hall context.
Table materials and lighting communicate wood, metal, rubber, plastics, lamps, painted art, and ball reflections without hiding play.
The ball remains readable against the playfield during high-speed motion.
HUD or DMD shows score, ball number, tilt warnings, lock count, multiball state, and major awards.
Rendering exposes performance controls or fallbacks for heavy visual effects.
The game uses Vibekit audio context helpers and safely no-ops when Web Audio is unavailable.
Flippers, slingshots, bumpers, rollovers, targets, plunger, lock, drain, trough, tilt warning, and tilt have distinct audio cues.
The table includes a subtle music bed that does not mask mechanical pinball sounds.
Lamps and inserts communicate current objectives, progress, multiball, jackpots, warnings, and bonus count.
DMD messages announce start, skill shot, awards, locks, multiball, jackpots, tilt, bonus, game over, and leaderboard eligibility.
Major hits combine audio, lamp flash, score or DMD update, and optional impulse without harming ball tracking.
Music and sound-effect settings persist locally through Vibekit storage helpers.
Audio levels, input preferences, initials, accessibility choices, and last-used options persist with Zod validation.
Active session state tracks score, ball number, active balls, tilt, locks, multiball, bonus, run start, and table id.
The game stores a local high-score list for offline play and local score chasing.
Completed games submit score, initials, table id, duration, ball count, tilt count, multiball count, jackpot count, counters, and build version.
The server rejects impossible or malformed leaderboard score summaries.
Leaderboard routes rate-limit repeated submissions using Vibekit server helpers or equivalent Upstash-backed primitives.
The global leaderboard uses a dedicated VibePinball Upstash Redis resource and never shares another project's store.
Leaderboard outages do not block local play, local scores, or completed-run UI.
The app uses Next.js App Router with client-owned simulation and server routes limited to online services.
Game logic, physics mapping, scoring, input, persistence, and leaderboard validation use strict TypeScript boundaries.
The render module owns Three.js scene setup, assets, materials, camera, resize, and mesh sync.
The physics module owns Rapier world setup, fixed steps, bodies, colliders, sensors, events, and device impulses.
The rules module consumes physics and input events and produces scoring, lamps, DMD, ball, tilt, bonus, and summary state.
Vibekit is used for shared math, RNG, storage, audio context lifecycle, server KV, and rate-limit primitives where applicable.
Asset loading fails visibly in development and degrades clearly in production.
Vercel deployment requires green verification, a healthy preview, and dedicated storage before leaderboard features are enabled.
Pure scoring, rules, tilt, bonus, input mapping, storage, and leaderboard validation logic have Vitest coverage.
Physics harnesses verify flipper activation, drain detection, sensors, plunger ranges, nudge accumulation, and multiball accounting where feasible.
Playwright verifies nonblank 3D canvas pixels, table framing, visible ball after launch, and resize safety.
Smoke coverage exercises keyboard, touch emulation, and gamepad mapping where browser automation allows it.
Leaderboard API tests cover valid submission, invalid schema, impossible score, rate limit, unavailable KV, and read response shape.
Release candidates pass a playtest gate for session length, readability, multiball, drains, nudging, and browser health.
At 80 percent GDD coverage, the fun-factor audit converts P0 or P1 gaps into release-blocking work.
V1 excludes table editor, layout editor, scripting tools, and public creation workflow.
V1 excludes second tables, themed variants, and alternate layouts.
V1 excludes mods, skins marketplace, user-generated assets, table sharing, and paid cosmetic systems.
V1 excludes deep modern wizard rules, long mission stacks, complex mode stacking, and advanced rule chains.
V1 excludes coin-door, operator-menu, service diagnostic, maintenance, and real-money operation simulation.
V1 excludes replay-verified leaderboard validation and full anti-cheat replay adjudication.
